 'An Injustice to One is an Injustice to All': Students Hold Vigil to Commemorate Nolan Wells
 By
 Tevis Pixton 
 and Sophia Riley Sim 
 Oct 30, 2026 9:56 pm 
 Reading time: about 5 minutes
 Roughly 70 students attended a vigil for Nolan Wells on Ho Plaza Wednesday night to honor his life, contest the lack of criminal charges pursued after an investigation into his death and call for social and institutional reform for racial justice and equality. 
 The event organizers, Cornell NAACP , Cornell Black Students United and SoulAAn Nation , also aim to establish a shrine in Ujamaa Residential College , a historically Black program house, in Wells’ memory. 
 18-year-old Wells , a Black student-athlete who played on the football team at Southwest Mississippi Community College , went missing on July 4 after celebrating Independence Day with friends on a remote barrier island off the southern shore of Mississippi. His body was found near the shore two days later.
 The circumstances surrounding his death have drawn suspicion from his family and the public alike, with much of the public speculation focused on the fact that Wells was the only Black friend in the group and the only person who did not return from the trip.
 Though a grand jury concluded that there was no evidence of criminal conduct in the case, Wells’ legal team alleges that the investigation has been mishandled on the grounds of racial bias.
 Takiya Henson ’27, Cornell NAACP juvenile justice chair, began Wednesday’s vigil with Wells’ story and a moment of silence. 
 “There were too many inconsistencies with this case,” Henson said. “Nolan’s life mattered. He didn’t have the chance to graduate college. He didn’t have the chance to meet the love of his life. He didn’t have the chance to pursue his dreams, have kids, to grow up. He didn’t have the chance to have his life start. He was taken away too young. So at this time, I invite everyone who is able to stand with us to remember Nolan.”
 Suspicions about racial bias in the Wells case are rooted in Mississippi’s long history of racial violence. Last September, the body of 21-year-old Demartravion “Trey” Reed was found hanging from a tree on the Delta State University campus in Cleveland, Mississippi, sparking similar conversations about racially motivated crimes.
 Athena Holloway ’27, president of Cornell NAACP, followed the moment of silence with a speech about racial injustice and her organization’s goals. 
 “Too often, the deaths of young Black people are dismissed, downplayed or inadequately investigated unless we demand answers,” Holloway said. “Our movement in this case is part of our ongoing commitment to make sure those answers are pursued with urgency and respect for Black life.”
 Alongside Holloway, representatives from BSU, SoulAAn Nation — a student organization dedicated to celebrating African American culture — and The Black Ivy Pre-Law Society spoke during the vigil. Common desires of broad justice system reform, racial equality and building a stronger Black community within the University connected their addresses. 
 Kennedy Young ’28, co-president of BSU and publicity chair of Cornell NAACP, led attendees in a call-and-response chant honoring Wells. Young called out, “Say his name,” prompting the crowd to respond, “Nolan Wells,” repeatedly.
 One speaker, Jocelyn Swavy ’28, vice president of SoulAAn Nation, shared her poetry at the vigil.
 “Take my flesh and make it into something you can sell, something you can own, something you can sit upon,” Swavy read. “But when you reach for my throat, know that you will not make me into nothing, because I was somebody, and we were somebody and we will not be forgotten.”
 During Swavy’s poem, an attendee shouted out “shame” as she read the line: “How many mothers must identify their children before this country recognizes that we’re somebody’s child, that we are loved, that we deserve to be loved?”
 Domaine Waysome ’28, a member of The Black Ivy Pre-Law Society, also spoke about feeling disillusioned by the justice system. 
 “Regardless of how much we are told to trust the justice system, it will continue to fail us as Black individuals in the United States,” Waysome said. 
 After the speeches, Cornell NAACP passed out sticky notes to attendees and asked them to write their response to the question: “What did Nolan Wells deserve?” Responses were added to a community board that will be donated to Ujamaa to build Well’s shrine. Flowers, notes and other momentos will also be donated to Ujamaa. 
 “[The community board] is a forum for people to share, but also for people to read and understand that they're not alone,” Young said in an interview with The Sun. 
 The effort is a part of a larger initiative to “regain [Ujamaa’s] culture,” Holloway said. 
 The residential college has experienced a decrease in its Black student population, while cultural artwork has also been removed from the dorm’s walls, Holloway said. She hopes to make greater use of the residential college to build community and create a space that reflects and celebrates the Black community, including the shrine for Wells.
 Attendees were also invited to donate to the Wells family GoFundMe , a fundraiser for the family’s funeral and legal expenses and the cost of an independent investigation into Wells’ death. 
 The Wells family and its legal team have indicated that they will continue to pursue answers in the death of Wells, with the support of the NAACP. 
 As the vigil concluded, Young gave a final message to the Cornell student body in an interview with The Sun. 
 “An injustice to one is an injustice to all,” Young said. “While the victim looks like me, if we live in a society where people are subject to these institutions that allow injustices like that to happen, … none of us are safe.”
 Tevis Pixton Tevis Pixton is a member of the class of 2029 in the College of Arts and Sciences. He is a news contributor and can be reached at tmp86@cornell.edu.
 Sophia Riley Sim Sophia Riley Sim is a member of the Class of 2028 in the Brooks School of Public Policy. She is a senior writer in the news department and a staff photographer. She can be reached at ssim@cornellsun.com.
